summary: Describes AES-XCBC-PRF-128, a pseudo-random function derived from the Advanced Encryption Standard that IPsec implementations may want to use with IKE. It is a proposed standard that has been replaced by RFC 4434.

plainLanguage.summary: Secret keys need to be mixed into fresh random-looking values. This describes a recipe that uses AES for the mixing in the IPsec key-setup process. RFC 4434 has replaced it.

questions: how does ipsec generate encryption keys
subtitle: Using AES to generate pseudo-random key material for IPsec key exchange.

tldr.problem: IKE (Internet Key Exchange) needs a pseudo-random function (PRF) to derive encryption keys, but existing 96-bit PRFs produce shorter keys that are weaker than desired.
tldr.mechanism: AES-XCBC-PRF-128 uses the AES-XCBC-MAC algorithm (normally truncated to 96 bits) but outputs the full 128-bit value without truncation, producing longer, stronger key material.
tldr.outcome: This gives IPsec implementations an option to use AES for generating key material with full 128-bit strength. RFC 4434 replaced this document.

today: RFC 3664 is Proposed Standard and was obsoleted by RFC 4434. The full 128-bit PRF output provides stronger key derivation than the 96-bit truncated version.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
AES-XCBC-PRF-128 is a pseudo-random function (PRF) derived from the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES). It generates key material that IKE uses to derive encryption and authentication keys for IPsec.

The function is based on AES-XCBC-MAC, a message authentication code algorithm. Normally, AES-XCBC-MAC produces a 96-bit output that is truncated from a 128-bit internal value. For this PRF, the truncation step is omitted, yielding the full 128-bit output. This provides stronger key material than a 96-bit PRF would.
sections.plainLanguage: IPsec needs to generate secret keys from a master secret. This describes how to use AES to do that mixing in a way that produces strong keys.

sections.title: The Algorithm
sections.content:
The AES-XCBC-PRF-128 algorithm is identical to AES-XCBC-MAC except that the truncation step is not performed. That is, the output is the full 128-bit value produced by the algorithm, with no further processing.

Test vectors from AES-XCBC-MAC can be used to verify the implementation, specifically those labeled as "AES-XCBC-MAC" rather than "AES-XCBC-MAC-96". The latter are truncated to 96 bits and are not suitable for verifying the full 128-bit PRF.
sections.plainLanguage: Take the AES scrambler, run the input through it, and output all 128 bits of the result.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security of AES-XCBC-PRF-128 is based on the strength of the AES algorithm. At the time of writing, there are no known practical cryptographic attacks against AES or AES-XCBC-MAC-PRF.

Like any cryptographic algorithm, its strength depends on the security of the key management mechanism, the strength of the secret key, and the correctness of implementations in all participating systems. The full 128-bit MAC value is used, not any truncated version.
sections.plainLanguage: AES is a well-tested scrambler, and this way of using it has no known weaknesses. Make sure the secret key is kept secret and the code is correct.

references.text: Frankel, S. and H. Herbert, "The AES-XCBC-MAC-96 Algorithm and Its Use With IPsec", RFC 3566, September 2003.
